'''''Anemone coronaria''''', the '''poppy anemone''',{{sfn|BSBI|2007}} or '''garden anemone''',<ref name="t483">{{cite web |title=garden anemone |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/108378/anemone-coronaria/details |access-date=2026-08-20}}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the buttercup [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Ranunculaceae]], native to the [[Mediterranean region]].

==Description==
''Anemone coronaria'' is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial]] [[tuberous]] plant growing to {{cvt|20-40|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall, rarely to {{cvt|60|cm|in|abbr=on}}, spreading to {{cvt|15-23|cm|in|abbr=on}}, with a basal rosette of a few leaves, the leaves with three leaflets, each leaflet deeply lobed. The flowers which bloom from April to June are borne singly on a tall stem with a whorl of small leaves just below the flower; the flower is 3–8 cm in diameter, with 5–8 red (but may be white or blue) showy [[petal]]-like [[tepal]]s and a black centre. The [[pollen]] is dry, has an unsculpted [[:wikt:exine|exine]], is less than 40µm in diameter, and is usually deposited within 1.5 m of its source. This central mound consists of tightly packed [[pistils]] in the centre, with a crown-like ring of [[stamens]] surrounding this, giving the species its [[specific epithet]] ''coronaria''.{{sfn|Johnston|2008}} The flowers produce 200–300 seeds.{{sfn|Laura|Allavena|2007}} The plants form hard black tubers as storage organs.{{sfn|MBG|2017}}

Aside from its flowers resembling [[poppy|poppies]], the red single wild form flowers resemble the flowers of the red single wild form of ''[[Ranunculus asiaticus]]''. Although widely called the 'poppy anemone' and sometimes rendered simply 'poppy' in English translations of Arabic sources,{{citation needed|date=August 2026}} ''A. coronaria'' is an anemone (Ranunculaceae), not a poppy (Papaveraceae); the corn poppy it resembles is ''Papaver rhoeas'', called khashkhash in Arabic.

== Etymology ==
''Anemone coronaria'' means crown anemone, referring to the central crown of the flower. The genus name ''Anemone'' and the English "windflower" are conventionally derived from the Greek ánemos ("wind"), the etymology reflected in the common name for some species in the genus. The binomial was established by [[Linnaeus]] in [[Species Plantarum]] (1753), making it the most recent of the plant's names.

In [[Hebrew]], the anemone is ''[[:he:כלנית מצויה|kalanit metzuya]]''. "Kalanit" comes from the Hebrew word {{Lang|he-Latn|kala}} ({{Lang|he|כלה}}) which means "[[bride]]", "metzuya" means "common". The kalanit earned its name because of its beauty and majesty, evoking a bride on her wedding day.<ref>[http://www.wildflowers.co.il/hebrew/plant.asp?ID=272 Anemone coronaria] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090504130015/http://www.wildflowers.co.il/hebrew/plant.asp?ID=272 |date=4 May 2009 }} in WildFlowers.co.il ([[Hebrew]]).</ref> In Israel, after the rainfall, the Negev Desert is blanketed in red due to the plethora of ''Anemone coronaria'', while wild flowers in the northern part of the country, such as the Galilee, sport a variety of other colours.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Why Israel’s north blooms in many colours while the Negev turns red, scientists find |url=https://www.ynetnews.com/environment/article/rjfsi4fezg}}</ref>

One proposed source of the name traces back to the Mesopotamian shepherd-god, [[Tammuz (deity)|Tammuz]], (Sumerian [[Dumuzid]]), a deity of fertility and vegetation, whose [[Phoenician language|Phoenician]] epithet was "Nea'man".<ref name="histsyria">{{Cite book| last = Hitti| first = Philip K.| title = History of Syria| access-date = 2020-07-02| date = 1951| url = https://archive.org/details/HistoryOfSyria-PhilipK.Hitti/page/n137|page=117}}</ref> Tammuz is generally considered to have been drawn into the Greek pantheon as [[Adonis]], who died of his wounds while hunting wild boar. The deity is transformed into a flower, stained by the blood of Adonis.<ref name="histsyria" /> Tammuz's Phoenician epithet "Nea'man" argued by Philip Hitti to be both the source of the Arabic "an-Nu'man" ({{Lang|ar|النُعمان}}) which came through Syriac, and of "anemone" which came through Greek.<ref name="histsyria" />

Another possible source of the name is [[Al-Nu'man III ibn al-Mundhir|An-Nu'man III Bin Al-Munthir]], the last [[Lakhmids|Lakhmid]] king of [[Al-Hirah]] (582–c.602 AD) and a [[Nestorian Christian]]. According to legend, the flower thrived on An-Nu'man's grave, after his death. He was deposed and put to death on the orders of the [[Sasanian]] king [[Khosrow II]], c. 602, paralleling the death and rebirth of [[Adonis]].

In Standard Arabic the flower is šaqā'iq an-nuʿmān (شَقائِق النُعْمان). The literal sense of šaqā'iq is debated: it is the plural of šaqīqa ("full sister"), so the phrase is often read as "the siblings/kin of Nu'man", while the common "wounds of Nu'man" reading is a poetic gloss drawing on nuʿmān as a pre-Islamic word for "blood" or "red". 

==Taxonomy==
''Anemone coronaria'' is the [[type species]] of the genus ''Anemone''.<ref name="IPNI">{{cite web |title=Anemone |website=International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/330847-2 |access-date=2026-08-20}}</ref>{{sfn|Hoot et al|2012}} Within the genus ''[[Anemone]]'', ''A. coronaria'' is therefore placed in the [[Autonym (botany)|autonymic]] [[subgenus]] ''Anemone'', [[section (botany)|section]] ''Anemone'', [[Subsection (botany)|subsection]] ''Anemone'', and is one of five species making up [[series (botany)|series]] ''Anemone'', together with ''[[Anemone hortensis]]'' <small>L.</small>, ''Anemone palmata'' <small>L.</small>, ''Anemone pavonina'' <small>Lam.</small> and ''Anemone somaliensis'' <small>Hepper</small>. Within the series ''A. coronaria'' is [[sister group|sister]] to ''A. somaliensis''. This series is a [[clade]] of Mediterranean tuberous anemones.{{sfn|Hoot et al|2012}}

==Distribution and habitat==
[[Mediterranean]] [[littoral]], from Greece, Albania, southern Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Northern Arabia to the [[Sinai Peninsula]]<!--NB part of Western Asia, not North Africa, in the WGSRPD used for plant distributions--> with sporadic extension east to Iran and west along the Mediterranean shores of Italy, southern France and North Africa.<ref name="POWO_708314-1">{{cite web |title=''Anemone coronaria'' L. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:708314-1 |access-date=2021-09-25 }}</ref>{{sfn|Laura|Allavena|2007}}{{sfn|MBG|2017}} 

Although they have been nurtured for two millenia, including early mention of cultivation by Pliny the Elder in ancient Rome, they still exist as well as wild flowers, particularly in Israel, southern Turkey, Syria, and Greece.<ref name="Fun">{{Cite web |title=Fun Facts About Anemones |url=https://flowermag.com/anemone-flower-symbolism-and-trivia/}}</ref><ref name="SCA">{{Cite web |title=Some Cultivated Anemones and their Histories |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/45126633.pdf}}</ref> 

==Ecology==
The flowers bloom in winter to early spring in the plant's native Mediterranean range (later, in spring, where grown in cooler climates). It is cross pollinated by bees, flies and beetles, which can carry pollen over long distances.{{sfn|Laura|Allavena|2007}} Certain colours of ''A. coronaria'' attract one insect over another; both honey bees and mining bees are attracted to both white and purplish blue, while flies prefer only white.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MDPI: Flower Colour Polymorphism, Pollination Modes, Breeding System and Gene Flow in ''Anemone coronaria'' |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/9/3/397}}</ref> Scarab beetles show an overwhelming preference for red ''A. coronaria'', which is also pollinated by other insects, such as honeybees.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pollination ecology of the red ''Anemone coronaria'' (Ranunculaceae): honeybees may select for early flowering |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/23531070_Pollination_ecology_of_the_red_Anemone_coronaria_Ranunculaceae_honeybees_may_select_for_early_flowering}}</ref>

''Anemone coronaria'' was introduced into England prior to 1596, being described in [[John Gerard]]'s ''Herball'', first published in 1597 and was popular during the time of [[Elizabeth I of England|Queen Elizabeth I]]; Thomas Johnson's enlarged and corrected edition appeared in 1633. By the beginning of the eighteenth century, breeders in France and Italy had already considerably improved the range of colours available.{{sfn|Laura|Allavena|2007}}

''Anemone coronaria'' is widely grown for its decorative flowers, and has a [[hardiness zone|hardiness]] of [[USDA]] zones 7–10, preferring full sun to part shade. Although perennial in its native climate, ''A. coronaria'' is usually grown as an [[annual plant|annual]] in cooler climates, from tubers. Planting is usually in the autumn if kept in pots in a greenhouse through the winter or in the ground in spring once the risk of frost has passed.{{sfn|MBG|2017}}

===Cultivars===
Modern cultivars have very large flowers, with diameters of {{Convert abbreviated|8-10|cm}} and a wide range of bright and pastel colours, in addition to two toned varieties. The centre is usually black, but may be pale green in white varieties. The stems may be as tall as {{Convert abbreviated|40-50|cm}}, and each plant may produce 13–15 blooms.{{sfn|Laura|Allavena|2007}}

Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been selected and named, the most popular including the De Caen (single) and St Brigid (semi-double and double) groups of cultivars.{{sfn|GW|2017}} The De Caen group are hybrids cultivated in the districts of [[Caen]] and [[Bayeux]] in France in the 18th century,{{sfn|MBG|2017}} and include 'Bicolor' (red with white), 'Blue Poppy' (blue), 'Mr Fokker' (purple), 'Sylphide' (deep pink) and 'The Bride' (white). Referred to as poppy anemones because they superficially resemble the true poppy (''Papaver''). St. Brigid cultivars originated in Ireland, and named after that country's saint, they include 'Lord Lieutenant' (purple blue) and 'The Governor' (red).{{sfn|Gardenia|2017}} In addition to these large groups, there are two minor groups, Rissoana which is very rustic and early blooming (November) and Grassensis with large double flowers that bloom in the spring.{{sfn|Laura|Allavena|2007}}

==Symbolism==

=== Greek ===
The Adonis myth tells of how the goddess Aphrodite is the lover of a handsome youth, Adonis. When the latter is gored by a wild boar, Aphrodite rushes to help him. Finding him lifeless, she transforms him by turning his blood into the red anemone.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The New Cabinet Cyclopaedia |url=https://www.google.co.il/books/edition/A_Handy_Book_of_Reference_on_All_Subject/UeFDAQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=greek+mythology+book+including+adonis&pg=PA36&printsec=frontcover}}</ref> This amorous and calamitous significance also exists on the island of Cyprus and has earned the plant its presence in various European art forms.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Flora of Cyprus |url=https://floraofcyprus.com/ranunculales/anemone-coronaria/}}</ref>

=== English ===
In remembrance of the Adonis myth, red anemones are known as Adonis flowers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Britannica: anemone |url=https://www.britannica.com/plant/anemone}}</ref>

=== Christian ===
The flowers have traditionally been associated with the term "lily of the field" used in the Christian [[Beatitudes]]. Matthew 6 compares lilies of the field to Solomon, stating that they effortlessly trump even the great king in terms of splendid garb.<ref name="Fun"/>

Mention of a solitary, brilliant red anemone which made its journey from the Holy Land to Pisa in the twelfth century during the Second Crusade exists. Its luminousness was attributed to the flower's absorption of Christian blood spilled in the soil of the Holy Land during battle, but can practically be explained by the fact that Anemones in Israel (''Anemone coronaria'') are a more dazzling he than their counterpart in Italy (''Anemone pavonina'').<ref name="SCA"/>

=== Renaissance ===
Wealthy gardeners prized flowers from exotic lands, and showcased them in their gardens. Botanical pursuits were lauded. Anemones were one of the flowers most showcased during this era, both in Italy and further north in Europe, i.e. Austria, Belgium, and Holland. Hence the flower came to symbolize affluence.<ref name="SCA"/>

=== Israel ===
In 2013 ''Anemone coronaria'' was elected as the [[Floral emblem|national flower]] of the [[Israel|State of Israel]], in a poll arranged by the [[Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel]] ({{Lang|he|החברה להגנת הטבע}}) and [[Ynet]].<ref name="Ynet-2013">[http://www.ynet.co.il/articles/0,7340,L-4457684,00.html הכלנית: הזוכה בתחרות "הפרח של ישראל"], [[ynet]], 25 November 2013.</ref> Each year in Israel there is a [[Darom Adom|month-long festival]] to celebrate the blooming of the red anemones.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/60000-flock-to-south-where-fields-torched-by-incendiary-ballons-now-bloom/|title=60,000 flock to south where fields torched by incendiary balloons now bloom|last=staff|first=T. O. I.|website=[[The Times of Israel]]|language=en-US|access-date=2019-02-02 |issn=0040-7909}}</ref> In addition to admiring the flowers, the event includes guided nature and history excursions in the area, cooking and painting classes, herb, spice, vegetable,  and fruit markets, and entertainment such as musical performances. In 2016, Shoshana Damari performed her iconic song "Kalaniyot", a tribute to red anemones.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Darom Adom |url=https://www.jpost.com/magazine/darom-adom-443852}}</ref>

After 7 October 2023 after the killing of Israelis and foreign nationals by Hamas, the festival went on hiatus, or at least changed; in February 2024, the festival was cancelled, but The International Christian Embassy in Jerusalem, together with the KKL-JNF, pledged to plant 1,200 memorial trees in the area, dedicated to the 1,200 victims of 7 October. Meanwhile, the blooms offered a sense of life's renewal, resilience, and strength after so much anguish.<ref>{{Cite web |title=On backdrop of burnt Israeli south, first red anemones of season bloom |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-782451}}</ref> In January 2025, it was temporarily renamed "Darom B'Lev" (The South in our Hearts), as opposed to "Darom Adom" (The Red South). At this point, the event focused on supporting families whose loved ones were being held hostage in Gaza.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Darom Adom Festival to be held in solidarity with hostage families |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-837311}}</ref> In February 2026, after all hostages, both dead and alive, were secured from Gaza, the festival returned, but under its changed 2024 name. Picnic baskets were sold, workshops returned, and even horseback riding and hot air balloon rides were offered, giving a sense of rejuvenation to the region.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gaza envelope hosts Darom BaLev for 2nd year as anemones carpet south |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/gaza-envelope-hosts-darom-balev-for-2nd-year-as-anemones-carpet-south/}}</ref>

'''Art'''

The flower was the subject of Israeli art way prior to 7 October, a positive symbol of passion and the emotion evoked by nature. Its strong colours were also indicative of the harmony inherent in cooperative dwellings. But sometimes the colour evoked a sense of foreboding, due to its association with the "Red Alert" warning when there were threats in the area.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Red Alert |url=https://www.imj.org.il/en/exhibitions/red-alert}}</ref> After 7 October, it has been used profusely in Israeli art, symbolizing both loss and hope, as in the exhibit "Anemones before the Rain", depicting both a water cascade and 5,000 clay anemones, homemade by Israeli volunteers throughout the country.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Installation "Anemones Before the Rain". |url=https://www.runi.ac.il/en/whats-up-lobby/news/the-installation-anemones-before-the-rain-is-on-display-at-reichman-university-in-commemoration-of-the-one-year-anniversary-of-the-war-s-outbreak}}</ref>
